ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: The retina is a thin, layered neural tissue lining the back of the eye that converts light into electrical signals for vision. Its health is essential for clear sight and is vulnerable to systemic and ocular diseases.

sections.p: The retina is the light‑sensing sheet of the eye, about 0.2 mm thick, containing photoreceptors, interneurons, and ganglion cells that form the optic nerve.
b: Four neuronal layers: photoreceptors, bipolar, ganglion, and supporting layers
Divided into central (fovea) and peripheral zones

sections.p: It lines the inner surface of the globe, adherent to the choroid and separated from the vitreous by the internal limiting membrane.
b: Fovea centralis: cone‑dense, responsible for high‑resolution vision
Peripheral retina: rod‑dense, important for dim‑light vision

sections.p: Anteriorly contacts the vitreous body; posteriorly rests on the vascular choroid; the optic disc is the exit point for retinal ganglion axons.
b: Optic disc lacks photoreceptors – creates physiological blind spot
Macula lies 3 mm temporal to the optic disc

sections.p: Dual supply: central retinal artery (inner retina) and choroidal circulation (outer retina).
b: Inner retina: supplied by central retinal artery branches
Outer retina (photoreceptors): supplied by choroidal vessels

sections.p: Retinal ganglion cells send axons through the optic nerve to the lateral geniculate nucleus and visual cortex.
b: Central retinal vein drains into the cavernous sinus
Retinal nerve fiber layer thickness is a marker of glaucoma

sections.p: Photoreceptors transduce photons into electrical impulses; bipolar cells relay signals to ganglion cells, which fire action potentials to the brain.
b: Cones detect color, fine detail, and function best in bright light

sections.p: Retinal pathology can cause irreversible vision loss; early recognition is vital, especially in low‑resource settings where treatable infections are common.
b: Diabetic retinopathy – microvascular leakage, proliferative disease
CMV retinitis – seen in advanced HIV, requires antiviral therapy

t.b: What structural abnormality is present? – Detects hemorrhages, exudates, detachments; if unavailable, use indirect ophthalmoscopy with a torch.
What is the thickness of retinal layers? – Quantifies macular edema; if unavailable, rely on clinical grading of edema.
What is the pattern of vascular leakage? – Identifies neovascularisation; if unavailable, use clinical signs of proliferative disease.

sections.p: Key points to remember for exams and bedside assessment.
b: Fovea contains only cones; peripheral retina contains mostly rods
Central retinal artery occlusion causes sudden painless vision loss with a cherry‑red spot
Macular edema presents with central blurring and thickened retina on OCT

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden painless loss of vision (possible central retinal artery occlusion)
Flashing lights with new floaters (risk of retinal detachment)
Rapidly worsening blurry vision in diabetes (proliferative retinopathy)

faq.q: Why do rods face away from incoming light?
faq.a: Rods’ outer segments point toward the choroid, allowing light to pass through overlying layers before reaching them.

faq.q: What is the significance of the optic disc’s blind spot?
faq.a: No photoreceptors are present, so this area cannot detect light; the brain fills in the gap during normal vision.

faq.q: How does HIV affect the retina?
faq.a: Advanced immunosuppression can lead to CMV retinitis, causing necrotizing lesions and rapid vision loss.
